The '''Harish-Chandra integral''' is a concept from [[integral calculus]] that originated in the study of [[harmonic analysis]] on [[Lie group]]s. Closely related is the '''Harish-Chandra formula''' which is used to evaluate the integral.

The integrals are named after the Indian mathematician [[Harish-Chandra]], who proved in 1957 the so-called Harish-Chandra formula.<ref>{{cite journal|author=[[Harish-Chandra]] |title=Differential Operators on a Semisimple Lie Algebra |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |year=1957 |volume=79 |publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press |pages=87–120 |doi=10.2307/2372387 |jstor=2372387 }}</ref> Today, the integral and its associated formula find applications in many fields, such as [[representation theory]], [[random matrix theory]] and [[quantum field theory]].

A special case is the formula for integrals over the [[unitary group]] which was independently discovered in 1980 by [[Claude Itzykson]] and [[Jean-Bernard Zuber]] and applied to quantum field theory. The integral over the unitary group is also referred to as the '''Harish-Chandra–Itzykson–Zuber integral'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |first1=Claude |last1=Itzykson |first2=Jean-Bernard |last2=Zuber |title=The planar approximation. II. |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=21 |pages=411–421|date=1980 |DOI=10.1063/1.524438}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>G</math> be a connected, semisimple [[compact Lie group]] and let <math>\mathrm{d}g</math> be the [[Haar measure|Haar probability measure]]. Let  <math>\mathfrak{g} = \operatorname{Lie}(G)</math> be its [[Lie algebra]] and <math>\mathfrak{t} \subset \mathfrak{g}</math> be the [[Cartan subalgebra]] (or its complexification <math>\mathfrak{t} \subset \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}}</math>).

The '''Harish-Chandra integral''' is the function<ref name="CmS">{{cite journal |first=Colin |last=McSwiggen |title=A New Proof of Harish-Chandra's Integral Formula |journal=Commun. Math. Phys.|volume=365 |pages=239–253 |date=2019 |issue=1 |doi=10.1007/s00220-018-3259-9 |arxiv=1712.03995 |bibcode=2019CMaPh.365..239M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=Colin |last=McSwiggen |title=The Harish-Chandra integral: An introduction with examples |journal=Enseign. Math. |volume=67 |date=2021 |number=3/4 |pages=229–299 |doi=10.4171/lem/1017 |arxiv=1806.11155 }}</ref>
:<math>H(x,y):=\int_G e^{\langle \operatorname{Ad}_g x, y \rangle} \mathrm{d}g</math>
for <math>x, y \in \mathfrak{t} </math>, where <math>\operatorname{Ad}</math> denotes the adjoint representation, and <math>\langle \cdot {,} \cdot \rangle</math> is the [[Killing form]].

== Harish-Chandra formula ==
Let <math>G</math> be connected and semisimple, and let <math>R^+</math> denote the positive root system of <math>\mathfrak{t}</math>. Then<ref name="CmS" />
:<math>\Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}(x)\Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}(y)\int_G e^{\langle \operatorname{Ad}_gx,y\rangle}\mathrm{d}g=\frac{[\![\Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}, \Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}]\!]}{|W|}\sum\limits_{w\in W}\varepsilon(w)e^{\langle w(x),y \rangle}</math>,
where
*<math>W</math> is the [[Weyl group]] acting on <math>\mathfrak{t}</math>,
*<math>\Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}(x) := \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} \langle \alpha, x \rangle</math> is a polynomial function called the discriminant,
*<math>\varepsilon(w) := (-1)^{|w|}</math> is the signature,
*<math>[\![\Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}, \Delta_{\mathfrak{t}}]\!]</math> is an inner product that extends the killing form to polynomial functions defined in the following way: If <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are polynomial functions on the real Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, write <math>p(x) = \sum{\beta} c_{\beta} x^{\beta}</math> in real coordinates <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math>, where <math>n = \dim \mathfrak{g}</math>. The associated differential operator is 
::<math>p(\partial) = \sum_{\beta} c_{\beta} \frac{\partial^{|\beta|}}{\partial x^{\beta}}.</math>
:The bilinear form <math>[[p, q]]</math> is defined by applying the differential operator <math>p(\partial)</math> to <math>q(x)</math> then evaluating the result at the zero, i.e.
::<math>[[p, q]] := p(\partial)q(x) \bigg|_{x = 0}.</math>
